utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-97-25-T; the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours,

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Mr. Masovic, there's just a couple of matters I'd like to clear up from yesterday. In the transcript it appears that when I asked you the question as to how many bodies were exhumed from Foca municipality and the answer was 436; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. 430 bodies were exhumed in the territory of the municipality of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, you referred to the document 240/5 which is the list of people you have recorded missing at your office and were last seen at the Foca KP Dom, and I asked you some further questions as to whether or not you had on record anyone else that is still recorded as missing and last seen at the KP Dom, and you stated there were about 35 people that weren't on that list.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said at least 35 more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And just so it's clear for the record, what is the reason why they're not on the list that you've provided to the Court?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These 35 at least are not on the list because we could not confirm from at least two independent sources that they were last seen alive at the KP Dom Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And before we finished yesterday, we were discussing the method in which people reported either friends or other people they knew missing to your office during the war. You mentioned that you received written reports from local authorities, the police, the military, the Red Cross. You also received on some occasions witness statements and intelligence reports. You also mentioned that you received oral reports from friends and family of the missing person.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I know you've discussed this in relation to the details taken in relation to your exhumation records, but can you clearly outline the information that was recorded by either you or your staff from the friends or family that contacted your office as to the details of the missing person.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information was taken over by my staff in Sarajevo headquarters and also in the regional offices throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina where these offices operated. And also we got some of our information from the records of the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what information would you ask your staff to record on the computer when these reports were made?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name and surname of the missing person, father's name, date of birth, place of birth, place of residence, place and date of disappearance of the said person, then also a designation that was used by the delegates of the ICRC. If some of their staff visited a certain person at a camp or prison, there was a so-called BAS number that was assigned to such a person. And then also there was information included about the person since the person went missing. For example, there would be remarks stating that, in the meantime, that particular person had been exhumed, and that closed the case as far as that person was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And yesterday you mentioned two types of situations where someone may come to your office or rang up your office where they provided information as to one particular person that went missing or a large number of people that they knew of that went missing, and you stated that in the cases where someone had information about a large number of people going missing, you would personally speak to those people.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. If these were characteristic cases, namely, cases of a massive disappearance of persons at a given location, then I would directly talk to the witness or family member who had such knowledge. In other cases, my officials worked on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you recorded that information or spoke to that person, how did you record it and when did it go on to the database?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was recorded in the internal files, the statements; and then the core of these statements would go into the computer database, the name, surname, father's name, things like that which I already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And of the documentary information that you received at your office, how long after would that be placed into the computer database after it was received?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same day, if it was a simple case, that is to say, if one missing person had been reported. And if it was only the first part, namely the initial stage of the conflict, when it was not possible to enter the date on the same day, then the maximum deadline had to be between 15 to 30 days before such data were actually entered in the database.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after that data had been entered from the written document, where would that go? Would that be filed?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are not classical files. All these documents have been preserved, though, and they are in the offices at the headquarters of the state commission in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to the other situation where a person reported someone missing but had no real further information about large numbers of others, you mentioned that your staff would take those reports?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And would they enter that information straight onto the computer, or would they record it in hard copy, then transfer it at a later time?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first period they were entered directly into the computer, and over the last three years, all family members fill out a form in their own hand by themselves, including additional pieces of information. During my testimony yesterday, I pointed out that it is quite certain that all 23.000 persons who are missing in Bosnia-Herzegovina are dead by now. That is why we enter data concerning characteristic details like the clothes that the persons wore when they went missing. We need this as additional information assisting the identification of such persons if they are found. So for the past three years, family members have been filling out this questionnaire where they describe the clothes that the person wore, jewellery, and perhaps even some anthropological characteristics; whether the person concerned is tall, short, whether the person's bones had been fractured in the past, things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, I would be interested to know what is the volume of such inquiries or people filling out forms. It might give us some idea of how much weight to be given to this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, you've mentioned that people in the last three years have provided further information on these forms. About how many of the people that have reported people missing have done that? You've mentioned that there's a figure of 23.000, and I assume you're talking about Bosnia-Herzegovina; 23.000 missing in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: It wasn't clear to me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I add something? The number of persons who went missing who are recorded is 27.719; however, in various morgues all over Bosnia-Herzegovina there were over 4.000 victims that haven't been identified so far. That is why I'm speaking about the number of 23.000, although the grand total is 27.719.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreters are having trouble with the speed at which you speak, so could you please speak -- especially when you're giving figures, so would you please speak a bit more slowly. What we want to know is how many people have filled out these forms or have made inquiries from you over the last three years?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give a precise figure, but I think that by now we have over 3.000 questionnaires that were filled out by closest family members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the 23.000 figure relates to missing Bosnian Muslims or people of all ethnicity from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Persons of all ethnicity from Bosnia, all citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how many of them are Bosnian Muslim citizens?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over 95 per cent are Bosnian Muslims. About 4 per cent are Bosnian Serbs, a bit less than 1 per cent are Bosnian Croats, and a small number -- I think about 260-something persons belong to the category of other ethnic groups that lived in the territory of the former Yugoslavia or possibly some other European states.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And once a person has been recorded missing with the state commission, apart from these forms that were filled out by some people, were any further inquiries made to update this information to confirm the accuracy of the initial reports?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day, every day this information is updated in order to confirm the accuracy of the information we receive on the ground. If a witness or a family member comes by a new piece of information or if our investigators come by a new piece of information, and also if there are extra findings concerning the identification of witnesses, every day information is updated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you cross check your information with any other records, such as the Red Cross or any other sources, once you've recorded people missing?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would like to point out that their information is scantier because they record missing persons only if family members have reported them as such, whereas we have broader criteria, and I already explained at the beginning of my testimony who are all the persons and organisations that can submit information to us in order to register persons as missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after the person has been recorded with your office in the last eight years or so, do you contact the local municipal authorities to inquire as to whether or not this person is still recorded missing, or update the information? Local authorities from where they formerly resided.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since local municipal authorities have very close contact with family members, these are persons who are not staying at their homes now. They're displaced all over the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather, all over Europe and the world. They have close contact with family members, and from time to time, say every six months or every year, we contact the local authorities of individual municipalities in order to check whether in the meantime the situation has perhaps changed in terms of the number of missing persons and other data concerning such persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, we've been talking generally here about your general method, but in relation to these particular lists, the lists of the missing people from Foca municipality and the people missing from Foca KP Dom, in preparation for your testimony today, have you conducted any further checks on top of what you normally do in relation to missing persons recorded at your office?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the material that is related to missing persons that has been submitted to the OTP has been checked out with the local authorities of the municipality of Foca, as compared to the information held by the ICRC, and also in correlation with statements made by former inmates at the KP Dom if we're talking about that prison, or also statements given by witnesses who had not been at the KP Dom Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in your experience with the State Commission for the Tracing of Missing Persons, how many false reports are you aware of, or are you aware of any, in relation to missing persons recorded at your office?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were attempts to report some persons as missing, although they did not go missing. However, we would usually consult local police authorities and then realise that this was false reporting. I can perhaps remember three such attempts over the past eight or nine years that I have been heading these offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, based on the documents that you've provided, 240/4 and 240/5, in relation to missing people from Foca and the Foca KP Dom, I'm going to ask you some general questions about them. How many people have been reported as still missing from Foca? What is the number?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of missing persons is 730. However, the persons -- the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. number of actually missing persons needs to include an additional figure of 413 Bosniak and Bosnian Croats. There has been testimony to the effect that they were killed; however, their bodies have not been located yet. In accordance with local Bosnian regulations, they are still considered to be missing. So the number in Foca now is 730 - we have no information about them as to whether they are dead or alive - plus 413 persons whom witnesses claim they had seen dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And of the 730 that are on your missing list, can you say what ethnicity these people are?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of these 730, I think that a vast, vast majority, over 90 per cent, are Bosnian Muslims, and there's a small percentage of Bosnian Croats. However, in the territory of the municipality of Foca before the war, between 1991 and 1992, there were about 100 Croats living there, so their percentage of missing persons is less than 1 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And of the 730 missing, how many of them are female?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that particular figure, so I'll have to look at this. 18 per cent, or 133 persons, are of the female sex.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And from your records, is it indicated what role these people played in the conflict, if any, if they were civilians, if they were soldiers, or do your records not show that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These records include civilians only.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you said in relation to a document 240/5, the document relating to missing persons last seen at KP Dom, that the 266 people you have recorded there are supported by two sources to that fact.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least two sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And of these 266 missing people, how many of them are supported by a source or a report from a family member; can you say?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all 266 were originally reported by family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what is the next most predominant source used to support this information? You said family member appears to be the most predominant source. What is the next most significant source?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, in terms of importance, we believe that the most important evidence is provided by co-inmates, that is to say, persons who spent some time at the KP Dom together with these persons at the KP Dom and were perhaps exchanged after that or released due to their age or other reasons. We believe that testimony given by such persons who were inmates at the KP Dom are the most important. Family members can say that their missing family member had been taken in the direction of the KP Dom; however, we do not necessarily know whether such a person ended up at the KP Dom. That is why we consider the testimony of former camp inmates to be the most reliable.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm afraid, sir, the interpreters are still having trouble with the speed at which you speak. They usually have a valid complaint about the speed at which I speak, but you are speaking more quickly than I am. So please, sir, do slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you say from the document how many of these 266 people have been reported as missing from the KP Dom by former inmates?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot give any precise information to that effect; however, a vast majority have been confirmed by former inmates. A relatively small -- a relatively big group of inmates was exchanged in October 1994 from the KP Dom in Foca and were taken to Sarajevo where they were exchanged at the confrontation line, so these inmates testified about that, namely, who out of these 266 spent some time with them at the KP Dom. Some of the inmates also testified that some of the persons who are on this list were allegedly taken out for an exchange, yet others were taken out to do some kind of work, to work in a mine, pick plums, et cetera. However, their families testified later, and we came to realise, that these persons had not been exchanged, that they had never appeared on territory that was held by government forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And apart from these two particular sources, the family member and former detainees, what other specific sources were used for this document?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The International Committee of the Red Cross is also a very relevant source of information about this in order to have a person considered missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were any documents used from the Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We don't know of such documents except in one case when we received from the ICRC one document titled something like "Prisoners reported by Serbian authorities but never seen or visited by ICRC representatives." That is the only document drafted by the ICRC based on data received from Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you look at the document 240/7 in your folder, is that the document you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely the document I've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you received that document from the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Where did you receive it?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with the Dayton Accords, a special working group of the ICRC was established which works on the tracing of missing persons in the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia, and one of the sessions of this working group handed this document over to us. It was also handed over to representatives of the Serbian commission so as to enable them to answer the question, "What happened to these people who are recorded as former inmates?" I note that many names are listed there, and only a part of the names refer to former inmates of the KP Dom Foca, whereas other persons listed there were imprisoned in other camps on the territory held by Bosnian Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when did you receive this document?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was at one of the sessions which took place two and a half, maybe even three or three and a half years ago. There have been, so far, about 15 sessions of this working group, and it was perhaps the fourth or the fifth session which handed this document over to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And at this working group, did the Red Cross explain the nature of the document and what it was to you and to the other members of the group?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were told that these persons were inmates recorded in Serbian prisons. And our commission also received a document containing names of Serbs who are believed to have gone missing, disappeared in camps which were controlled by legal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did the Red Cross representative explain how they received this information from the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly at this moment, but if I may say so, I know from some media, Serb media reports that I followed, that there was a polemic between Dragan Kalinic who was blamed for allegedly handing over this document to the ICRC in Geneva from the authorities of the KP Dom in Foca, but this is only something that I know from, from following press reports. I don't know how reliable that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you can now look at document 240/6. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was that prepared by your office?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what does that document show?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is actually an analysis of the previous document we discussed. After having reviewed all the names of prisoners reported by Serbian authorities, we made an additional effort to establish whether perhaps some of these people have survived and are still registered as missing. And we arrived at this document which contains the names of 90 persons who are still believed to be missing today and are registered as such by the state commission. And the overwhelming majority, perhaps all of them, are registered with the International Commission of the Red Cross, and we believe that other prisoners, those who are not on this list, have actually been exchanged. So this is a list of persons which have been reported by camp authorities on the 30th of August, 1992, and have not been exchanged or released in the period that followed, that is, until the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, this list is derived from the Red Cross list we just spoke about, 240/7, but this list only relates to people detained or notified as being detained at the Foca KP Dom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And just so that it's clear, are all of the people on this list recorded as still missing at the state commission?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are still believed and are still registered as missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we can go back to document 240/5, which is the list of missing and last seen at KP Dom, the 266 names, there's a column on the right-hand side of that document that states the month of disappearance of the particular individual. What does that, what does that refer to; the month of disappearance from where?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These indications of month in the special rubric denoted as the month of disappearance have been taken over from the ICRC database, which does not necessarily mean that it was the last time the person was seen. In some cases, persons were seen and taken to the KP Dom at a later date than the one indicated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So that information, if not all of it, comes from the Red Cross in relation to when they disappeared generally, rather than from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They originate from the Red Cross -- this information originates from the Red Cross, not the KP Dom. Those people have -- were reported, identified, on the 30th of August, 1992, and here in this rubric we see April or May indicated, and this is the month when they were taken away from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So the fact assumed or stated in this report that these people were in fact at the KP Dom, that doesn't come from the Red Cross in relation to -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is data generated by our commission, but it has been compared with other sources and checked against the database of the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How many of these -- or do you know the ethnicity of the 266 people in this list?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I read out all the names, I could give you my opinion, but I believe all of them are Bosnian Muslims. If you give me a second, I'll be able to answer that question. Yes, there is a Bosnian Croat, number 105, Mate Ivancic. I think that is the only recorded instance of a missing person of other ethnicity than Bosnian Muslim. There is also Krunoslav Marinovic, number 158. Those are the only two Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What was that second number?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 158, Marinovic, Krunoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Smith. I understand that the Prosecution's use of this list is twofold; one to show attack upon the Bosnian Muslim civilian population, but also in relation to appendix C, annex C. I'm not sure myself from the witness's answer whether we can rely upon all of these as having been in KP Dom. It may be that it just wasn't very clearly stated, but I think that there seems to be something not quite clearly linking them all to KP Dom. So far as annex C is concerned, I suppose we must go by the names. If they're the same name, we can assume that they were the one who was in KP Dom. But if you want us to go any further, I think you may have to get some further elucidation from the witness on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, if we look at this list, it states that you've recorded these people as missing from Foca municipality and last seen at KP Dom; and you've mentioned that to get this list, to form this list, you've relied on at least two sources to establish this fact as best that you can. The list, the list really relates to two factors; one, that the person -- that the people contained in this list are still missing today; and the second factor is that these people were at KP Dom, Foca KP Dom. In relation to the fact that these people were at Foca KP Dom during the war, do the two sources -- have you two sources that support that fact, or is it -- do you have -- or do the two sources relate to the two, the two Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. factors; one that they're missing, and one that they're at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say with a high degree of certainty that 266 persons who are on these -- on this list were really last seen in the KP Dom, and that has been confirmed by at least two different sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So just to be clear, those two sources that you refer to confirm that these 266, or each of the 266 were at, were at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you also -- it may be the same sources or it may be other sources, but is it the case that you also have two sources that confirm that each one of these individuals is now -- is still missing today?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. All of them are still on the list of missing persons. The number of missing persons who spent some time in the KP Dom is much, much higher than the number indicated on this list. This list contains only the names of people who continue to be missing today. And in addition to them, we have in our records information about a lot of other people who spent some time in KP Dom before being released, exchanged, before dying, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Masovic, I'd like you to look at an exhibit that's been used in this case. It's Prosecution Exhibit 55, and it's being supplied to you and it's in your folder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Does that contain the additional material now from the investigator which there has been some agreement between the parties on?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No, just Schedule C.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to study this list in relation to the records you have regarding missing people prior to coming to court?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had occasion to see this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in that light, is there anyone on that list that is not reported as still missing with the state commission? And we'll just take it name by name.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to analyse it name by name, but generally speaking, all these 29 persons are believed to be missing but with certain provisos that I would have to make now, explain now. There are some typographic errors and errors of other natures. With regard to some of these persons we have information to the effect that they're included in other lists of Foca residents who were killed, so they are not on this -- on that other list containing 730 names. So if we go name by name, number 1 is Alija Altoka, Salim Bico, number 2; Bico is the nickname of this person. Salim, sorry, is the nickname, and the real name is Hamed. If you -- I can look it up in the other list and tell you the number on that other list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, there's no need to do that, but I just will refer Your Honours to the other lists. Hamed Bico appears on 240/4, the large list, and also appears on 240/5, the KP Dom list that the witness has prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you go further down the list and relate which ones don't appear on your list?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the names are on our records, but on different lists. Some of them are on the list of missing persons, and others are on the lists of persons who were killed. According to the information we have and the testimony of witnesses, Alija Altoka, number 1; Eso Dzamalija, number 6; Esad Kiselica, number 12; Edin Krajcin, who is number 14; Hamid Ramovic, who is number 20; and Mithat Rikalo, number 22, were killed. I mentioned number 2, Salim Bico. There is an error on this list because Salim is the nickname of the man. And then also in number 5, Enko Cedic, Enko is shortened for Elvedin, and this person has been recorded with us as Elvedin Cedic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can stop you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And Your Honours, Elvedin Cedic appears on 240/4 and 240/5.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a number of individuals, Alija Altoka, number 1; Eso Dzamalija, number 6; and I believe Esad Kiselica, number 12; Edin Krajcin, number 14, and Hamed Ramovic, number 20, and Mithat Rikalo, number 22. Now, those names appear on the list of missing on 240/4 from Foca municipality, but they don't appear on the list 240/5 in relation to people missing from KP Dom. Now, in those cases, those six cases, other witnesses have testified that they were present at KP Dom and have not been seen since. Just assuming, assuming that's correct, do you know why they appear -- why you have them appearing on the list of 730 names and why they don't appear on the list relating to those missing and last seen at KP Dom? Is there an explanation for that, or not?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The explanation is simple. Regarding those six persons, we were unable to receive confirmation that they were last seen at the KP Dom from at least two sources. They have been confirmed, but they belong in the category of those people, of those 35 people I spoke about before, who have been confirmed by witnesses to have been seen at the KP Dom, but we failed to obtain a second confirmation from a different source. So we have confirmation from only one source, and we did not use it in that list of 266 persons who were last seen at the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I now can refer you to number 18, Omer Mujezinovic, his name doesn't appear on either list, 240/4 or 240/5. A witness has come to the court and stated that he believes the first name of Omer is a mistake, and the name of this person is Samir Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So Witness 111, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And that Samir was at the KP Dom and taken out. Do you have a Samir Mujezinovic on your list of missing and missing from KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. And if I may add, after we received this list, when we reviewed it and analysed it, we consulted several different sources, and the person under number 18, Omer Mujezinovic really lived in the territory of Foca before the war, but this man died in a car accident. So we have Samir Mujezinovic on our list, and we believe that the person who made this list of 29 persons made a mistake. The name that should be on the list is Samir Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if I can refer you to number 16, Fuad Mandzo, his name doesn't appear on either list. Do you have any information on a Fuad Mandzo at the state commission, other than a person not recorded as a missing person?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fuad Mandzo is one of the persons who has not been confirmed by two sources and who is on the list of persons who were killed which contains 413 names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And this Fuad Mandzo that you are talking about, what is his date of birth and his former residence?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the year of birth is 1959, and his former residence is the town of Foca, more precisely, the neighbourhood of Donje Polje, a predominately Muslim neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you have any information as to the circumstances of this particular person's death?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have such information available to me here, but it's possible that we in the commission do have some additional data on the cause of death. Fuad Mandzo is on the list of people who were killed, not on the list of missing persons, which seems to indicate that we have reliable information that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know how many Fuad Mandzos there are, and there were in the municipality of Foca?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there is only one person, and I'm saying this based on the 1991 census where there is only one person named Fuad Mandzo appearing on that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, if you can now look at Prosecution Exhibit 39, which is also in your folder. Now, have you had an opportunity to review this list before coming to court?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: This is a list of persons that the Prosecution allege have been detained at the KP Dom, and have been registered with the Red Cross. Is there anyone on that list that is not recorded as missing from Foca municipality, namely, your document 240/4?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that there are some persons like that. I would have to go through the list name by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the question -- perhaps if you don't go through the list name by name --

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, actually, I believe that all the persons on this list, there are no ordinal numbers here but I believe all these persons have been registered as missing with our commission, and I even think that all of them are on our list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that there are some people that have not been recorded as missing, and from reviewing your lists I have found ten individuals that don't appear on your list 240/5, which is still missing and disappeared from the KP Dom; and those individuals are Alija Altoka, Miralem Altoka, Omer Altoka, Fadil Divjan, Alija Dzelil, Izet Grosonja, Adil Krajcin, Dzemal Niksic, Hamid Ramovic, and Srnja Hidajet. They don't appear on 240/5, but those individuals do appear on 240/4. Assuming this information is correct, can you explain why these names do appear on your larger list but don't appear on this smaller list of 266 names?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because these people have not been confirmed by several independent persons as having last been seen at the KP Dom in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm just going to ask you a few questions about prisoner exchanges. By September 1992, about how many Bosnian Muslims were detained in detention centres in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just didn't understand the time you were referring to, I mean September 1992. At that time, I think that in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina over 10.000 Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats were detained in Serb prisons, especially in the area of Bosanski Krajina where the largest camps were Omarska, Keraterm, Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And from your records, is it indicated whether these people were soldiers or civilians, or can you not say?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A vast majority of these people were civilians, even civilians who were arrested far away from the confrontation lines, that is to say, deep in the territory that was held by the Serbs, that is to say, in towns where people actually lived, worked, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in relation to prisoner exchanges and prisoner releases, which was a large focus of your work during the war, have all of those exchanges or all of those -- and all of those releases, are they recorded by your office?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We recorded only part of the prisoners of war, that is to say, civilians deprived of their liberty. Actually, there are other state authorities that deal with the overall subject of inmates. We were only interested in a smaller number of inmates, namely those who we recorded as inmates in camps whose release was negotiated through our office in Sarajevo and our offices throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to Foca KP Dom, about how many people have you recorded as being either released or exchanged?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Released, usually unilaterally because of their age or sickness. We have recorded 44 persons who lived in the territory of Foca before the war, and then I think about 180 were exchanged, perhaps a bit more. Persons who were exchanged through negotiations with the appropriate Serb commission, and who lived in the territory of the municipality of Foca, namely, in the Foca prison during the war. There were also some imprisoned members of the Bosnian army. Some of them were taken prisoner in 1994, some in 1995, but they do not originate from Foca. At the moment when the war broke out, they lived in some other towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but they were deported to the camp in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I'm not referring to how many people have you recorded as being exchanged or released that formerly lived in Foca, I'm specifically directing the question to how many people do you have recorded having been exchanged or released from the Foca KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, according to our records, 44 were released from the camp, and a bit more than 230 were exchanged from the Foca KP Dom. However, including members of the army who were taken prisoner in 1994 and 1995, and who had not lived in Foca beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is it possible that releases and exchanges occurred from Foca KP Dom, and your commission would be unaware of it or not record it?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I should say that theoretically this is possible; however, all persons who got out of prison were treated by the first police stations that they came across in government-held territories, so these police stations submitted their reports to us. So I believe that there was no possibility for someone to get out of prison without having that recorded at our commission. Theoretically it is possible; however, if it so happened that a person was deported directly from the KP Dom to a third Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. country, a European country, and that that person did not contact anyone, even our embassy in that third European country or some other state authorities, then it is possible that the state commission had not recorded such a person, but this is theory, I imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you mentioned earlier in your evidence that the state commission, you were involved in the exchange of the prisoners of war --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were there some exchanges that you weren't involved in, prisoners of war, where your office would not be notified? And in particular, I'm referring to the 1992 period.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In certain situations, when certain private arrangements were made, for example, there were cases in the KP Dom Foca in particular that some people managed to get released from the KP Dom by paying a certain amount of money. In some cases, these were relatively high amounts of money, exceeding 30.000 German Deutschemark, I believe. So they were not involved in the legal procedure that had to be observed. That is to say, that approval had to be sought from our headquarters in Sarajevo in order to have the exchange carried out. So there are such possibilities of cases of persons who managed to get out, as we say, through private channels. To get out of prison, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you a few questions about the population movement of people from Foca in 1992. Are you in a position to say where people fled, in which direction generally, from the records that you received at the state commission after the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already in April, after the first armed conflicts broke out in the territory of Foca, the majority of the Bosnian Muslim population tried to get out in three directions, approximately. Some fled before the Serb forces along the Drina and Cehotina rivers towards Gorazde. Another part fled towards Trnovo, a small place near Sarajevo which at that time was under government force control, and yet another group tried to seek shelter by hiding in areas around Foca, approximately in the area of the Tjentiste, that were not easily accessible. So there are three groups that tried to get away in different directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the 1991 census shows that there are about 20.000, at least 20.000 Bosnian Muslims living in Foca in 1991. By the end of 1992, from your records, can you say about how many of these people were still living within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the end of 1992, there was only a small percentage of Bosnian Muslims left in Foca, and those were only people who were detained at the KP Dom. It is also possible that there were some individuals, not more than ten of them, who expressed their loyalty to the Serb authorities. Some of them were also members of the Serb army. So, by the end of 1992, a negligible number of Bosnian Muslims lived freely in the territory of the municipality of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And from your knowledge of the Foca area, and more particularly from the information you obtained from your records, can you say whether the Bosnian Muslim population or a part of it has started to return to Foca municipality, and if that has happened, when did that start?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The state commission does not have such information within its records because this goes beyond our jurisdiction; however, I personally inquired with the local authorities in Foca what the situation was in view of returns. The mayor of Foca told me that only 1.200 to 1.500 Bosnian Muslims returned to some parts of the municipality of Foca, primarily to the Bosnian Muslim villages. So I think that, in percentage terms, as compared to 1992, the percentage of persons who managed to return to their own homes does not exceed 8 per cent. This repatriation started only last year, as far as I know, because the territory of the town of Foca and the municipality of Foca was considered to be a dark hole, as we called it. Even we at the state commission considered it to be so. Even international representatives refrained from supporting us in our exhumations in the territory of the municipality of Foca. Truth to tell, that was not the only municipality where our access was impeded. There were other such municipalities, like Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can just stop you there. When you say a dark hole, are you referring to lack of cooperation with the authorities in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not establish any contact with the authorities. On the other side, our partner is the Serb commission, the Serb commission that does the same kind of work as we do. They are our partner. They are the ones who established contact with their own local authorities, with the police, those who are duty-bound to provide escort and Security Services to us from the inter-ethnic boundary line. The problem was that the international forces, the SFOR forces that were stationed in that area, very often suggested to us that it was still too early for us to do our job in the territory of the municipality of Foca. I can only speculate or engage in guesswork as to why it is so. However, it was a well-known fact that some of the persons who were publicly indicted by this Tribunal, and some of the persons who were considered to be on sealed indictments freely moved about the territory of the municipality of Foca practically all the way up to last year or the year before last.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If Your Honour would just excuse me for a moment. Your Honour, I have no further questions. I formally would like to tender some of these documents that have been referred to. I seek to tender 240/1, which is the map and the corresponding index that relates to the exhumation locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is that an ID number now so that we can give it a P number?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, yes Your Honour. So the map and the index. Secondly, 240/3, which is a list of the bodies exhumed within the Foca municipality, of identified people. I'd also like to tender 240/4, which is the list of people still missing from Foca municipality as recorded by the state commission; and 240/5, which is a list of people still missing and last seen at the KP Dom, which was prepared by the state commission; 240/6, which is a list of people detained at the KP Dom Foca as notified by the Bosnian Serb authorities to the Red Cross, which was prepared by the state commission; and 240/7, which is the original document that was given to the state commission by the Red Cross relating to detained people notified by the Serb authorities in their camps to the Red Cross. And they are the documents, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague Mr. Vasic has dealt with this subject matter, and he will be the one to cross-examine Mr. Masovic. We are not opposed to these documents except for two, that is, document 240/5. That is the list of 266 persons who were last seen in the KP Dom Foca. The Defence does not have any information or any proof, any papers that would show which are these two independent sources on the basis of which this list was compiled. We just have information from the witness that this list was compiled on the basis of two independent sources; however, we are not aware of which sources these are, nor do we manage to have any insight into all of this. And we could not check for ourselves whether these were indeed two independent sources. The other document that we're opposed to is I believe 240/7. That is a list that was confirmed, or rather, a list that is entitled "Confirmed by the authorities of Republika Srpska." Yes, by the authorities of Republika Srpska. Again, we haven't got any auxiliary documents. We haven't got any proof to corroborate this. Is this on the basis of something that was received in writing? On the basis of which information did the authorities of Republika Srpska compile this list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, now --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And also, I do apologise, that on the basis of that, the International Red Cross made up a list. So we haven't got any papers to corroborate that, either. The Defence would like to check that out, and then perhaps by the end of the Defence case, even, we could look into these two documents and see whether they could actually be entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just let me clear up the problems you have. In relation to 240/5, that's the KP Dom list, do you want to know the identity of the independent sources, or do you simply want to know the nature of them, such as, two different family members or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The witness spoke about two independent sources. We don't know which two independent sources were used, nor have we seen anything. I think that the Defence is entitled to see these documents to see why these persons were recorded as last being seen at the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you haven't answered my question. Do you want to know the identity of the sources or simply the nature? You want to see the documents themselves, I gather?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The nature of the documents, and from the nature of the documents we will be able to see the identity of the persons concerned, so it is the nature of the documents. I don't know whether these are only statements made by family members, or perhaps whether there is some document in writing. The Defence is not aware of this. As for all other documents, we agree; however, this is a highly relevant question for our case, and we would indeed like to see these sources on the basis of which this list was made up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in relation of the Red Cross, what is the nature of your objection to that? You said you haven't been over to check it out, but what is it that you seek?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the list that we got, it doesn't say anywhere that it was compiled by the International Red Cross and on the basis of information, et cetera. That's only contained in the title. We haven't got a shred of proof to corroborate this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But look, Mr. Bakrac, I'm trying to narrow the issue; I'm not trying to debate it with you. What you are seeking, are you, is some document from the Red Cross to say that that's the list that they have compiled, or are you seeking to know the information which the Red Cross had in order to compile it? I want to know how far back we have to inquire if your objection is upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we haven't got any proof here that would show that this list was obtained from the Red Cross, so we need evidence of that nature. And we also haven't got any proof that the authorities of Republika Srpska submitted such a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, please, let's deal one at a time. I'm trying to narrow the issues that you are raising. In relation to the Red Cross, would you be satisfied if a letter was produced from the Red Cross saying they had compiled it, or are you also seeking to know what information the Red Cross had in order to compile it? Now, that's a simple question. It should be provided with a simple answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it would be sufficient or, rather, the Defence would be satisfied if the International Red Cross were to confirm that they compiled this list of persons, and also if they stated the source on the basis of which this list is compiled. So it is sufficient if in one letter the Red Cross would confirm this list and the source on the basis of which this list had been compiled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, let's assume that, as I would believe to be the case, the Red Cross is relying upon notifications from hundreds of people to it that these people are missing. As I recall some evidence somewhere along the line in this case, the ICRC invited people to register missing people with them. Now, are you seeking to have those registrations as well? How far down to the basic facts are you seeking to have us go? Would it be sufficient, for example, if they said just that, that they relied upon notifications given to them by people that these persons were missing?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Perhaps we haven't understood each other properly. I really don't want us to use up this much of our time, and I am not doubting the authenticity of what the international -- of that which would be conveyed to us by the International Red Cross; however, this list does say, the heading says that this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I do want an answer Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to my question, and I think I am entitled to it. Do you want the Red Cross to identify the people who made the complaints or who gave them the notifications, or are you satisfied with a statement made by the Red Cross that that is what they relied upon in general terms, notifications by people that these persons were missing?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, we don't need identification of every person who sent an application or information. It is sufficient to say that this list was compiled on the basis of notifications given by a larger number of persons who came to the International Red Cross. However, please bear with me for one minute. There is a list that is sought to be tendered into evidence, and it speaks of a list that was obtained by the International Red Cross from the authorities of Republika Srpska. That is what the Defence is interested in, not every individual notification for every -- from every individual person, or we don't need a list of persons who came to the Red Cross. We're just interested in this list that was obtained from the authorities of Republika Srpska because it is being invoked, and we do not see it anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment. Mr. Smith, am I right in assuming that the document 240/7 is the one which the Red Cross received?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's right. The witness has said that he received it at a conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And until now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment. Just, let's get them clear. So what is it you need, then, more than document 240/7? Do you doubt the authenticity of that as having been supplied by Republika Srpska to the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no information whatsoever about that, Your Honour. First of all, I wish to clarify whether this is the document that we received, that is to say, 240/7, whether that was the document that was compiled by the commission that is headed by this witness; or is that the authentic document that the witness received from the commission of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I suspect that is not the exact document; it's compiled from that document. So you want -- because part of it is in English. You want the actual document which the witness says he was given by an official of Republika Srpska, is that what you want, or a copy of it? Mr. Vasic is nodding his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. I now understand and have got narrowed the points you are taking, so I'll hear what Mr. Smith wants to say about these. Now, Mr. Smith, bearing in mind that we are relying upon thirdhand information here, and I'm not criticising you for that, in fact, we are very grateful it has been put in this form, but if there is a challenge to it, I think that the Defence is entitled to some further material. There should be no problem, should there, in obtaining from the Red Cross some document which describes in general terms the source of the information from which they compiled that list?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: There may be some difficulties, Your Honour, with the Red Cross in relation to gaining information for court purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, let me just say this to you about the Red Cross: There is a decision of the Tribunal which protects information which they obtained in very limited circumstances where they have been granted access to prison camps, and although the view that I took in that case was not quite that of the majority, I would not want in this case to try to depart from the majority's decision, but it is very limited. And the Red Cross, having invited this information and supplied the other, should surely be able to describe in general terms where they got that information from. I would like to say that it must be almost beyond reasonable doubt as a matter of common sense that they compiled it from information given to them by people whom they had invited to give them that information, and it was for this very sort of purpose. And if the ICRC wants to be difficult about that, they should go away and hang their heads in shame. So I don't think there should be any difficulty, really. And then you might like to tell them that the Trial Chamber takes a very firm view that they are negligent in their duties if they do not provide it, in very general terms, without identifying the people, but just describing the general sense -- in a general sense, where they got their information from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we will attempt to do that. But just to perhaps clear up the evidence, this witness has stated that the Red Cross -- he believes the Red Cross compiled -- he was told the Red Cross compiled this document from information that they received from Serb authorities notifying them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That they had people in their --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is that something that the ICRC would claim some form of privilege for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I cannot imagine it. Now, that is something which would resolve that particular problem with a great deal of ease. Similarly, all that the Defence wants in relation to 240/7 is a copy of the document itself that was provided to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: This is -- I mean, I can clarify with the witness, but this is the copy that was provided to him by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You mean this is a photostat copy of the actual document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, if you get that into evidence that should be sufficient, unless there's going to be a challenge to that piece of evidence, but it would certainly be sufficient for the document to get into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: This is a copy that he received from the Red Cross, a photocopy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You mean it had, it had the headings in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, how about clearing that up. I assumed that this was something which has been retyped to make it more convenient for the Tribunal, but if it is a copy of the exact document, then that should, I hope, resolve any problem from the Defence's point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, if you can look at your document 240/7, do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was that, was that the document that was provided to you by the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no, the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. This document was provided to him, I believe, by the Red Cross. The Red Cross compiled this document from information that they received from Republika Srpska authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you can clear that up, but that's not what Mr. Bakrac is after. He's after the document which the Red Cross received from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: There may or may not be one, Your Honour, and it's not clear -- this witness -- I'll ask him, but he may not be clear how the Red Cross compiled this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, see what you can find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, the document 240/7, is that the one that you received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've just seen the time. We'll take a break now until 11.40, but would you please discuss this with the witness. I think this is an appropriate case. It may be that we'll have to also ask the Red Cross as to what they received from Republika Srpska, but I think it's a justifiable inquiry. If you get the evidence from this witness it will probably be sufficient to get this document into evidence, but it may be a fair enough line of inquiry for the Defence to follow up to have a copy of whatever it was the Red Cross received from Republika Srpska. We'll adjourn now till 11.40 and I regret we've run over time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, the document 240/7, who gave you that document?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ICRC, the International Commission of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is that an exact copy of the document that was given to you?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a photocopy of the original document handed over to us by the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So it was handed over to you in English?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you received this document at a conference; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the title of the conference?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Working Group of the ICRC, established, I believe, on the 1st of March, 1996, as one of the institutions envisaged by the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how many other people were at this conference?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On average, more than 20 persons attend, including members of the association of family members of missing persons from all over the federation, which means Bosnian Muslim, Bosnian Croat, and members from the Republic of Croatia, and also of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the members were from --

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also Yugoslavia, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the members were from the respective commissions for tracing of missing persons, is that correct, some of the representatives?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Delegations of the parties were extended to include people from other ministries, such as the ministry of the police, ministry of the Defence, and I believe the ministry of health as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And representatives from the Serb authorities, Bosnian Republika Srpska authorities, they received a copy of this document as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. They received a copy of this document, too. In fact, they received the original of this document, just as we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you also receive a document from the Red Cross in relation to Bosnian Serb and Bosnian Croat detainees in Bosnian Muslim prisons during the war?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we received a document listing, I think, a total of 20 names of Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats believed to be -- to have gone missing during the conflict, and notified or recorded by the legal authorities of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did the Red Cross state what the purpose of handing these documents to each of the representatives from the various governments, what the purpose was in doing that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The task of that working group of the ICRC was to accelerate the flow of information about the fate of those 20.000 missing persons in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the priority in that task was on those persons who were reported by those legal authorities to have been imprisoned because it was considered to be the fastest way to learn about the fate of these people who these legal authorities admitted had been imprisoned as opposed to other missing persons who went missing in various villages and towns in whose cases it was sometimes very difficult to establish what had become of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did the Red Cross representative explain which people within the respective authorities provided notification that these detainees were in their detention centres?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Red Cross never shared that information with us or any other of the parties which participate in the work of the working group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during that conference, did any representative from the Republika Srpska object to this document or state that it's false or have any comment as to its authenticity when it was handed out?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no objections to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, the last question you asked, I don't think quite covers it. You asked did the Red Cross representatives explain Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which people within the respective authorities provided notification. What we're interested in knowing is whether the Red Cross revealed either the identity of their sources generally, or whether they gave some general description of their sources; in other words, whether it was beyond their various authorities, and when notifications were made directly to the ICRC. That's what I think we got to get down to. That is the point, as I understand it, of the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you understand that question from the Judge? Did the Red Cross representative explain or reveal whether or not this information had come from Republika Srpska authorities or people outside of the government or military structure, namely, friends and families?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, neither in this nor in other similar cases, because there have been other documents given to us by the ICRC which related to some other detention camps. The International Red Cross did not reveal and will not reveal information as to the origin of the document. On the contrary, the ICRC, in keeping with its mandate, keeps this information in confidence and did not share it with us. They simply made available this, to us this list of people who have been registered in various prisons, and it is our task to determine the fate of these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have they at any stage given a general description of the sources of their information? In other words, without revealing any particular person, have they described it as being from local authorities and persons who have registered missing persons; or have they just given you no information at all?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. No information at all, apart from what is indicated in the very title of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Smith, that does not bode well for any inquiry you may make of the ICRC, but you might make it clear to them when you do make an inquiry that we do not understand that to be within the terms of the decision in Simic, and that we would hope that they would be able to give us at least some general description without revealing particular sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps if I can just follow up with one specific question. The title of the document is "list of detainees notified by the authorities," and then underneath it has Republika Srpska. Did they say who these authorities were, whether it was a military authority, a police authority, or local authority?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the terminology that we used at that particular session and other sessions of the working group, we -- the term was "prison authorities." I don't know whether the term "prison authorities" is adequate; the usual way to put it is "prison administration," but that is the term we took over from the International Red Cross, and that term is "prison authorities."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I hope that is just enough, Your Honour, to establish the reliability of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It may be, depending on what Mr. Bakrac wants to say about it, but it is unfortunate that the Red Cross seems to believe that it is above giving any assistance to the very authorities who have to inquire into these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to this document, Your Honour, I would just submit that perhaps there's a reasonable degree of reliability to it, to its authenticity, and now it's a question of weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's what I -- that's my present view, subject to anything Mr. Bakrac wants to say. But as I say, it would be sufficient to get the document into evidence, but what weight we give to it is another matter. Are there any other questions you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's the 240/7. You will ask the Red Cross for a general statement in relation to 240/6, that they did provide that information, and you could ask them to identify in general terms the same sort of -- same sort of general terms, the source.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and 240/6 and /7, /6 is derived from 240/7, so it is actually the same source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Bakrac wants a statement that it did come from the Red Cross. I'm not sure that this is going to take the matter very much further because we've got the evidence from the witness, but we should at least ask them to state that they did give the witness, or at least to his commission, that particular information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: We will do that, Your Honour. And Your Honour, in relation to 240/5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: -- where the Defence has some objection to it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you see, that depended upon the commission getting information from two independent sources. You might be able to ask the witness what was the nature of the sources, which he might be able to tell us now, but the objection went further than that; they wanted to see the documents which were in the commission's possession as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can only say that, in terms of reliability, the witness comes from an organisation whose main purpose is to record missing persons and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You don't have to emphasise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But I'm trying to avoid an unnecessary amount of friction over an issue which may easily be cured. I don't think, despite the time I've been here, I've quite adopted the continental suggestion of consensus on everything. At some stage, judicial organisations have to make decisions. But if we can get at least a consensus, it would be better; it will prevent appeal points, if I may put it that way, Mr. Smith. So see what you can do to at least get a general description of who those sources would be, and then you might like to ask him what is involved in producing the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, you explained earlier how your records are processed and how you record missing persons. In relation to this particular list, the 266, how many of those people that are listed as missing have been supported or have been recorded as missing from a family member?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no, I'm sorry. That's not what I'm after. Ask Mr. Masovic first whether he can give us a general description of what the sources were, and then we'll get down to the more difficult problems of particular cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to this list, Mr. Masovic, 240/5, what were the -- all of the sources that were used to produce that list?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to inmates, and I underline "inmates," all the statements are based on the experience of inmates who were released or exchanged. However, not all testimony was directed directly to our commission. Some testimonies and statements were given to a family member who then informed us. Some testimony reached local authorities for exchanges, some to police authorities, military authorities, et cetera, and in a certain number of cases the camp inmates themselves, at the moment of their release or exchange, gave us statements at our headquarters in Sarajevo as to which inmates remained behind at the camp and who was last seen at the camp.
