utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As far as the other victim is concerned, Halid Konjo, he was recognised by his wife, according to the report, on the basis of his Seiko watch, a yellow-gold wedding band, and also it says here on the basis of four gold teeth in his upper jaw, and also something between the gold teeth as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And a woven belt as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, yes. A brown belt, knitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Again, the Defence wanted to see whether this report matched the forensic report. What was mentioned there was that a black belt was found, not a brown one. Also, the same was mentioned in the forensic report of the expert's team of the university clinical centre in Tuzla. In addition to that, in this forensic expertise, another thing is mentioned in the dental status. During the post-mortem, a bridge was found in position 16 to 25, that is to say, more than four teeth. Can you help us clarify these discrepancies related to Halid Konjo?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not a dentist, but I'll try. It's quite obvious what this is all about. A bridge goes for -- is longer than the number of teeth that it includes. I was not engaged in this post-mortem. I'm not qualified for that. I don't know what 16 and 25 means, actually. I mean, forensics experts would have to be asked about this after all. What is obvious is that there were only four gold teeth; however, the bridge that holds these teeth spans a bigger part of the mouth than that where only four teeth are.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the expertise, these four gold teeth are not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just ask that my friend indicate the document that he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That would be helpful, I think, Mr. Vasic. If I may say so, you left one matter up in the air, and that is when you asked how this man's father-in-law could have identified him on the basis of the few things you said, referred to. Nobody could suggest that each of these particular items was by itself sufficient to identify anyone. The basis upon which an identification would be made, I suggest to you, would be the fact that each of them existed together, rather like the definition of circumstantial evidence. You have a number of very thin strands which, when woven together, become a very strong piece of rope. It's no good taking each particular incident and saying, well, this belt was described as brown by one person and black by another. That's easily explicable by the fact that it had been left out in the elements for a very long time. Anything that's left out could quite well end up brown, and people may identify it in different ways. I really don't know whether this very minor detail that you're going into is giving us any assistance. If there's something really substantial, you go for it, but I think we're going to spend an awfully long time dealing with these minor matters, and in the end get nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was just thinking about what people were shown during this identification process because this does not correspond with what the original report said, so I was just wondering what these people were actually shown subsequently. But I shall not proceed with this line of questioning any further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I don't want you to stop if you've got something worthwhile going on with. You had not made it clear, at least not to me, that that was what you were after. You seem to be simply drawing attention to minor discrepancies in the descriptions. If you want to know what these persons who identified the people were actually shown, by all means, that's a very valid line of cross-examination. Don't stop. All I want to do is get forward and not dwell on minor inconsistencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday in response to my learned friend's question you talked about the site of Mazoce, and you said that a woman, a relative of one of the victims, drew your attention to the fact that all the houses of the persons who moved out were burned, whereas the houses of those who were found on that site were burned down. Can you tell us how many houses there are in the village of Mazoce?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what the daughter of one of the killed persons told me. I cannot remember precisely. What could be seen in that area was about 20 houses that are not concentrated in the same place. They are scattered about throughout the village, that is to say, in an area that I think would be about one kilometre by one kilometre, perhaps even less. This is mountainous terrain towards Montenegro, so houses are scattered around the hills, and they can be noticed from a particular site. Specifically from this site near the Orthodox Serb cemetery, one can notice that there are at least 20 houses that belong to the village of Mazoce.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the site of the Serb cemetery. Was Mazoce a mixed village, or was it a purely Serb village or a purely Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a mixed village for sure because precisely while we were working on the exhumation, one of the local Bosnian Serbs came up to us who is certainly older than 65. And when this victim's daughter asked what happened -- I think she even used his name, and I can't remember the name now. She asked him what had happened, and this was his answer, approximately: "Some kind of soldiers came in. I really don't know anything about this." I don't know how accurately this can be interpreted, but this is the language that was used by the local Serbs in that area. So that was his area, that was his answer: "Lots of soldiers, some kind of soldiers came in, and I don't know anything else." That was the end of their conversation, and I went with that lady towards our vehicle, and there was no further dialogue between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you check what this lady said, that only some houses were burned and others were not?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, absolutely not. We are interested in persons, people, missing persons, not in who committed crimes, who torched houses. The commission that I head does not deal in such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I have one more question for you related to this exhumation of Murat Crneta and Halid Konjo. How far away is that site from the front line that was there in 1992? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I really am not. During the war I was not in that area, so I cannot give you a precise answer how far away this is from the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in response to my learned friend's question, you said that in 90 per cent of all cases there were mass liquidations of Muslims in this area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the Serb forces would enter villages, all of those who were in the villages were liquidated, or a vast majority of them. Very seldom did it happen that anyone would survive these mass executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by "mass execution"?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the narrowest sense of the word, it meant that the villagers from a particular village or hamlet were assembled together at a particular place and then executed there by automatic weapons. And if we give a more extensive interpretation, then it involves the search of houses, barns, and other facilities in that village, and all those who are found hiding in these buildings are executed on the spot. So in one village, for example, in Jelec, if you take a look at this map that we made for this trial, you will see that in a relatively small area in a certain number of villages, a rather large number of people were liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If we look at annex 2 of the report P240/1, I can note that in only 19 out of 156 sites mentioned, more than five victims were found in one place. Is that 90 per cent?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that the figure you mentioned is correct; however, I repeat once again, mass executions mean the liquidation of people in their houses, at their homes, at the same time. At the moment when soldiers enter a village, they liquidate the entire population they find there. If you look at the first group -- or rather, the second group where at 53 sites, 161 victims were found, what do you notice? The site of the village of Paunci, that's the second group, number one, two, three, four, five, six. And then you can see that at the weekend cottage of Hasan Balic, three victims were killed. At Karabegovic, Alivada [phoen], one person was killed. At the Karabegovic house that is in that same meadow, one victim was found. Then in Jusufovic Salko's house, in the immediate vicinity three victims were found. In Frasto Adila's barn, one victim was killed, et cetera, et cetera

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Slow down please. Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned a few different types of buildings and sites within a small circle, houses that are close to one another, a barn, a meadow, et cetera, that is why I talked about mass executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: However, this would not fit into your narrower interpretation, that they were assembled at one point?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. In this case, there are no cases of this nature that have been registered, that in a narrower site we found 50, 60, to 100 victims as was the case in other places in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially in Bosanska Krajina and Eastern Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, I have to state that in the barn in Ratine, according to eyewitness statements, 24 persons were executed. And also nine persons in the village of Mazoce that we spoke of a few minutes ago, and I was present at that exhumation. And then seven persons in the village of Previla, and these are indeed mass executions with five or more victims involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the village of Previla now. Is this village now in the Croat Muslim federation?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by the Croat Muslim federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is Previla within the Republika Srpska or the Croat Muslim federation now, the village of Previla?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the Muslim Croat federation is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That part of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina that is not Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, you mean the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise; the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think Previla right now is in the area of the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I cannot maintain that with 100 per cent certainty, but I think that it is in the area of the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In response to my learned friend's question today, you spoke about a list of 413 persons -- 430 persons that are mentioned as dead by witnesses. Were these bodies exhumed?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not a single one of these 413 - four one three - persons was not exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are these persons registered as missing in your documents?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the broader sense of the word, they are missing. Actually de jure, they are considered to be missing because the fact of their death has never been established either by a court or by forensics experts, that is to say doctors who are authorised to establish someone's death, coroners. They are missing; de facto, they could be considered different in that respect from those 730 persons as compared to these 413 persons for which witnesses claim that they are dead, that they have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, according to the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what is the period of time that has to elapse after the end of a war in order to proclaim a person dead after he or she had been missing for a certain period of time? Are you aware of any such period?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local laws of the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina have left every family member the right to determine that point in time when that person's relative was considered to be dead. There is a Court procedure involved, meaning that certain persons have to prove in civil proceedings that their relative is deceased. I don't know exactly what the requirements are, but I think they have to bring witnesses to court who were present during that person's death, or to point out circumstances that unequivocally show that the mentioned person had died.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm afraid that it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's probably a good time for the break. I can tell you that in the Australia the period after which there is a presumption of death is seven years, but I don't know if that applies in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We'll resume tomorrow at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
